triage.name: Chalazion
triage.reason: Painless eyelid nodule distinguished from hordeolum by history and exam; a straightforward but instructive eyelid lesion case.

exam: term 'Extraocular movements full' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Adults are most commonly affected, but it can occur at any age
Slightly more common in adults with rosacea or seborrheic dermatitis

chief_complaints.text: I have a bump on my eyelid
It doesn't hurt, but it's annoying and I can feel it when I blink
My vision is a little blurry on that side

hpi.duration: Present for 2 weeks to several months at presentation
hpi.progression: Slowly enlarges over weeks, then stabilizes; may fluctuate in size and can resolve spontaneously over months
hpi.location: Upper eyelid more often than lower; may be single or multiple
hpi.quality: Firm, round, rubbery nodule within the eyelid tissue; not attached to the overlying skin
hpi.severity: Mild; usually painless or only mildly tender
hpi.timing: Constant, non-fluctuating; not related to time of day

associated_symptoms.text: Blurred vision from the lid pressing on the eye

pertinent_negatives: Marked redness and warmth of the entire eyelid
Ulceration or bleeding of the lesion
Recent stye or infected eyelash follicle

argues_against: Painful red eye with photophobia suggests keratitis or uveitis
Ulcerated or bleeding lesion suggests malignancy
Loss of eyelashes suggests sebaceous carcinoma
Fever suggests infection such as orbital cellulitis

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with a painless eyelid lump noticed by a parent; often resolves with conservative management, but large lesions can cause ptosis or astigmatism.
A persistent eyelid nodule in an older adult should raise concern for malignancy, especially if it ulcerates, bleeds, or causes lash loss.
May be more prone to recurrent or secondarily infected chalazia, and healing may be slower.

general.severe: Ill-appearing with marked eyelid swelling and tenderness
general.critical: Toxic-appearing with fever and diffuse periorbital inflammation

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the eyelid with the patient looking down
findings.finding: Firm, round, rubbery nodule within the eyelid tissue, not attached to the overlying skin

findings.maneuver: Express the meibomian glands along the eyelid margin
findings.finding: Inspissated or turbid meibomian gland secretions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelid margins and lashes
findings.finding: Crusting and scaling of the eyelid margin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyelid margin and conjunctiva for discharge
Check visual acuity with a Snellen chart
findings.finding: Visual acuity normal or mildly reduced from the lid pressing on the eye

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to follow a finger in all directions of gaze
Shine a light into each eye
findings.finding: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyes from above and below
Palpate the preauricular and cervical lymph nodes

not_indicated.why: No role in a simple chalazion; a normal white count does not change management
Inflammatory markers are not needed for a localized eyelid nodule
Inflammatory markers are not needed for a localized eyelid nodule
Not part of the chalazion workup; check only if there is other reason to suspect undiagnosed diabetes
Not needed for a simple chalazion; reserve for suspected orbital or preseptal cellulitis
Not needed for a simple chalazion; reserve for suspected malignancy or orbital extension

decision_points: A chalazion is a clinical diagnosis; no laboratory or imaging test is required for a typical painless eyelid nodule.
If the lesion is painful, red, warm, or spreading, evaluate for hordeolum or preseptal/orbital cellulitis instead.
If the nodule persists beyond several weeks, recurs, ulcerates, bleeds, or causes lash loss, biopsy to exclude sebaceous carcinoma.
Refer to ophthalmology if vision is affected, the lesion is large or recurrent, or conservative management fails.

differential.name: Hordeolum (stye)
differential.why_considered: Both are acute eyelid nodules arising from the meibomian or Zeis glands, and a chalazion can follow a hordeolum.

history: Painful and tender from the start
May have had a similar episode before
exam: Tender, erythematous, warm nodule at the eyelid margin
May point and drain purulent material
Often a visible pustule at the lash line

differential.name: Sebaceous carcinoma
differential.why_considered: A malignant eyelid tumor that can mimic a chalazion, especially when it recurs or persists after treatment.
differential.trigger: A chalazion that recurs in the same location, persists beyond several weeks, or is associated with lash loss, ulceration, or bleeding

history: Recurrent 'chalazion' in the same spot after incision and curettage
exam: Ulceration or bleeding of the lesion
Diffuse eyelid thickening or a yellow mass
May have a concurrent eyelid margin lesion
imaging: Not routinely needed; orbital imaging if spread suspected

differential.name: Basal cell carcinoma
differential.why_considered: The most common eyelid malignancy; can present as a painless eyelid nodule.
differential.trigger: A pearly, ulcerated, or telangiectatic eyelid lesion that does not resolve

history: Slowly enlarging over months to years
History of sun exposure or prior skin cancer
exam: Pearly or translucent nodule with rolled edges
Loss of eyelashes if the margin is involved

differential.name: Squamous cell carcinoma
differential.why_considered: Another malignant eyelid tumor that can appear as a non-healing eyelid nodule or ulcer.
differential.trigger: A crusted, ulcerated, or bleeding eyelid lesion that fails to heal

history: Rapid growth compared with a chalazion
exam: Hyperkeratotic, crusted, or ulcerated plaque or nodule
May be tender or bleed easily

differential.name: Preseptal cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Eyelid swelling and redness can be mistaken for an inflamed chalazion.
differential.trigger: Diffuse eyelid swelling with fever or systemic symptoms

history: Recent eyelid trauma, insect bite, or sinus infection
exam: Diffuse, not localized, eyelid swelling and erythema
No proptosis, normal extraocular movements, normal vision
imaging: Orbital CT with contrast if orbital extension is suspected

differential.name: Orbital cellulitis
differential.why_considered: A sight-threatening and potentially life-threatening infection that can present with eyelid swelling.
differential.trigger: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, or vision loss with eyelid swelling

imaging: Orbital CT with contrast showing orbital fat stranding or abscess

differential.name: Epidermoid cyst
differential.why_considered: A benign, painless, round nodule that can occur on the eyelid skin.

history: May have had a punctum or prior drainage
exam: Superficial, mobile, dome-shaped nodule within the skin

differential.name: Molluscum contagiosum
differential.why_considered: A viral infection that can cause small, painless eyelid nodules.

history: May have similar lesions elsewhere on the body

severity.mild: Small, painless, firm eyelid nodule without significant swelling or visual disturbance; conservative management with warm compresses is appropriate.
severity.moderate: Larger nodule with noticeable eyelid swelling, mild tenderness, or mechanical ptosis causing blurred vision; may require incision and curettage or intralesional steroid injection.
severity.severe: Large, recurrent, or multiple chalazia causing significant ptosis, astigmatism, or visual impairment; may require surgical excision and evaluation for underlying meibomian gland dysfunction or malignancy.
severity.critical: Not applicable; a chalazion itself is not life-threatening. Secondary preseptal or orbital cellulitis can become critical, but that is a separate diagnosis.

red_flags.finding: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, or vision loss
red_flags.meaning: Suggests orbital cellulitis or an orbital mass; requires urgent imaging and ophthalmology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Fever with diffuse eyelid swelling and erythema
red_flags.meaning: Suggests preseptal or orbital cellulitis rather than a simple chalazion

red_flags.finding: Recurrence in the same location after incision and curettage, or persistence beyond several weeks
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for sebaceous carcinoma or other malignancy; biopsy is needed

red_flags.finding: Loss of eyelashes, ulceration, or bleeding of the lesion
red_flags.meaning: Concerning for malignancy, especially sebaceous carcinoma
Unusual for a chalazion; consider infection or malignancy

complications.name: Astigmatism and blurred vision
clues: Large chalazion pressing on the cornea
Blurred vision that improves with lid elevation

special_populations.differences: May present as a painless eyelid lump noticed by a parent; often resolves with conservative management, but large lesions can cause ptosis or astigmatism and amblyopia.
A persistent eyelid nodule should raise concern for malignancy, especially if it ulcerates, bleeds, or causes lash loss; lower threshold for biopsy.
May be more prone to recurrent or secondarily infected chalazia, and healing may be slower.

key_questions.question: How long have you had the bump, and how did it start?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days to weeks; a chalazion is subacute, whereas a hordeolum is acute over 1–3 days

key_questions.question: Does it hurt?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless or only mildly tender; marked pain suggests a hordeolum or infection

key_questions.question: Has it been getting bigger, staying the same, or coming and going?
key_questions.looking_for: Slow enlargement then stabilization, or fluctuation in size; rapid growth over days is atypical

key_questions.question: Have you had a stye or a bump like this before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior chalazion or hordeolum; recurrence in the same spot raises concern for malignancy

key_questions.question: Do you have blepharitis, rosacea, or seborrheic dermatitis?
key_questions.looking_for: Underlying meibomian gland dysfunction or skin disease that predisposes to chalazia

key_questions.question: Do you wear contact lenses?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact lens wear as a weak risk factor and a reason to advise lens hygiene

key_questions.question: Is your vision blurry on that side, and does it change when you lift the eyelid?
key_questions.looking_for: Blurred vision from the lid pressing on the cornea; vision loss or pain with eye movement is a red flag

key_questions.question: Any discharge from the eye, redness, or crusting of the lashes?
key_questions.looking_for: Purulent discharge suggests infection; crusting suggests blepharitis

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, or swelling that is spreading around the eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever with diffuse eyelid swelling suggests preseptal or orbital cellulitis

key_questions.question: Any double vision, bulging of the eye, or pain when you move your eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, or diplopia suggests orbital cellulitis or an orbital mass

key_questions.question: Has the lesion ulcerated, bled, or have you noticed loss of eyelashes?
key_questions.looking_for: Ulceration, bleeding, or madarosis raises concern for sebaceous carcinoma or other malignancy

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes or another condition that affects healing?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes may predispose to recurrent or secondarily infected chalazia

reasoning_points: A painless, firm, round eyelid nodule that has developed gradually over days to weeks
The nodule is within the eyelid tissue and not attached to the overlying skin
Absence of marked pain, diffuse redness, warmth, purulent discharge, and fever
Visual acuity is normal or only mildly reduced from the lid pressing on the eye
Extraocular movements are full and painless, with no proptosis
Risk factors such as blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, rosacea, or seborrheic dermatitis are present
The diagnosis is clinical; no laboratory or imaging test is required for a typical lesion
Malignancy is excluded when the lesion persists, recurs, ulcerates, bleeds, or causes lash loss

easy: Adult with a painless, firm eyelid nodule present for several weeks
Normal visual acuity and full, painless eye movements
medium: Mild tenderness and eyelid swelling that make it hard to distinguish from a hordeolum
Blurred vision from mechanical ptosis or astigmatism
Multiple or recurrent chalazia suggesting underlying meibomian gland dysfunction
Child with a painless eyelid lump noticed by a parent
hard: Older adult with a persistent eyelid nodule that recurs after incision and curettage, raising concern for sebaceous carcinoma
Lesion with ulceration, bleeding, or loss of eyelashes
Diffuse eyelid swelling with fever suggesting preseptal or orbital cellulitis
Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, or vision loss suggesting orbital cellulitis or an orbital mass
Rapidly growing lesion over days, which is atypical for a chalazion
